events.title: The Berlin Wall opens
events.description: East Germans begin crossing the border freely. The change becomes a powerful symbol of a changing Europe.

events.title: Hubble launches into orbit
events.description: The space telescope leaves Earth aboard Discovery. Its first images later reveal a flaw in the main mirror.

events.title: The Soviet Union breaks apart
events.description: Gorbachev resigns as Soviet president. Independent states take the place of the union.

what_happened_next.text:
You invested after the October crash. That fall was already part of the starting prices, so it is not a new loss inside your five-year portfolio. This detail changes how to read the whole story: a frightening recent event is different from a loss that happens after you buy.

Over the next five years, McDonald's led the seven choices and the US share basket nearly doubled. IBM ended below its starting value. A recovery in the wider market did not lift every company equally.

Meanwhile, the Berlin Wall opened in 1989. Hubble launched in 1990, and the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991. People watched enormous changes unfold without knowing exactly what would follow.

The outcome does not show that buying after every crash is easy or certain to work. An investor still had to choose among businesses with different risks. Even if someone correctly expected the market to recover, that would not tell them which individual company to choose or how long to wait.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: The sudden market crash raised fears about the economy. Technology competition and a possible Sony record deal were smaller parts of the news.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: What happened after you invested mattered. The crash before the start could shape feelings, but it was not a loss inside this five-year portfolio.
reflection.what_faded_away: One terrifying day could not tell you which company would do best over five years. Attention-grabbing advertisements offered no shortcut either.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody could know that McDonald’s would lead this set while IBM lost value. A famous company could still be a disappointing investment.
